text.p: Firefighters were gaining the upper hand on Monday over a stubborn wildfire that has been burning in California's scenic Los Padres National Forest for a week.

The fire, which has charred 14,300 acres (5,800 hectares) of trees and brush, was 95 percent contained with full containment predicted for Tuesday evening, said Kathy Good, a spokeswoman for the U.S. Forest Service.

The fire was burning in steep, rugged terrain just south of Big Sur, a popular hiking and camping area on the central California coast. The cause of the blaze, which broke out a week ago about 150 miles (240 km) south of San Francisco, has been confirmed as arson, Good said.

She said firefighters had made very good progress over the last two days and the fire's perimeter was now holding relatively steady. But she said there would probably be a "sizeable increase" in the size of the fire over the next 24 hours because firefighters were burning islands of vegetation to make the fire easier to control.

Firefighters were also working on reinforcing containment lines around the fire, she said. About 2,155 firefighters were battling the blaze, backed by 94 fire engines, 11 air tankers, 12 helicopters and 17 bulldozers.

Firefighters have come across four more houses scattered through the forest that were destroyed by the fire, Good said, increasing the number of homes lost to five, along with nine outbuildings, two travel trailers and two vehicles, she said.
Fire engines remained in position to protect 43 homes near the west side of the fire as a precautionary measure, Good said.
Six firefighters have been injured battling the blaze, officials said.
